one-check-per-line.why: all 4 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 4

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 4 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: I checked each verifier PASS/FAIL condition against the words of its expect line. Checks 1 and 2 stay within their lines. Their sample values only test left padding with fill, the default space, the target width and returning s unchanged. Check 3 asks for a heading plus a description for each export, which is a reasonable reading of "a section". Check 4 breaks the criterion. The expect line says only "npm test passes", which an exit code of 0 already shows. The PASS condition also requires that "the output shows `# fail 0`". That is an exact-wording requirement the words do not force. Newer versions of `node --test` use the spec reporter, which prints "ℹ fail 0", so a passing run could be marked FAIL. That stricter check belongs under Advisory, not in PASS.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command in both briefs. Most of them are fine: `npm test` maps to the `node --test` script, and the Check 1, Check 2 and Check 4 one-liners have valid syntax. Check 3 is the problem. It wraps the JavaScript in a double-quoted shell string and writes `new RegExp('\\b'+f+'\\b')`. Inside bash double quotes, `\\` turns into a single `\`, so Node receives `'\b'`. In a JS string that is a backspace character, not a regex word boundary. The pattern then never matches any README heading, so the check would print every export as "missing" even when the README is correct. The command runs, but not as intended: the shell escaping breaks the JavaScript it delivers, so a correct PR would fail. The criterion therefore fails for the verifier brief.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all three must_catch items against the briefs, and each one is handled.
1. Builder step 3 says "The README is already missing a section for `slugify`. Add a `## slugify(s)` section…" and also asks for a `## padLeft` section.
2. Verifier Check 3 prints the exports at the PR head. Its PASS line names "capitalize, slugify, truncate, padLeft", and it FAILs if "any exported function has no heading in README.md (for example slugify or padLeft)".
3. Verifier Check 1 calls `m.padLeft('42',5)` with no fill argument and expects "   42". It FAILs on a "default other than a single space".
A side note that doesn't affect this criterion: in Check 3, the `'\\b'` inside bash double quotes reaches JS as `'\b'`, which is a backspace character. The script could then report correct headings as missing. Even so, the check still lists the exports and FAILs when slugify has no section.

avoids-must-not.why: Must_not 1 holds. Check 3 fails whenever any export has no heading ("for example slugify or padLeft"), so a README with a padLeft section but no slugify section cannot pass. Checks 1 and 2 do not demand a one-character fill or a parameter count, and the multi-character fill case is only advisory. Must_not 2 breaks, though. Check 3's command is wrapped in bash double quotes, so `'\\b'` reaches JS as `'\b'`, which is a backspace character, not a word boundary. No heading can match, so every function is reported missing and even a correct README fails. That FAIL condition is stricter than line 3. Check 4 also requires the output to show `# fail 0`, which only appears in TAP reporter output. Node's spec reporter prints `ℹ fail 0` instead, so a passing `npm test` with exit 0 could still fail. That is stricter than "npm test passes".

methods-private.why: The builder brief gives the builder some of the verifier's probes. Step 2 hands it concrete inputs with expected outputs: "padLeft('42', 5, '0') === '00042' and padLeft('42', 5) === '   42'". The verifier's Check 1 uses those same two probes, inputs and expected results alike ("00042","   42"). Step 5 also has the builder compare `export function` names against the `##` headings in README.md, which is the logic of the verifier's Check 3 script. Telling the builder to run `npm test` and write its own tests is allowed. Shared input/expected-output pairs are not, because they show the builder exactly what the checker will test. So the builder brief carries verifier checks, and the criterion fails.
